title: Sweet Tooth, Big Brain: Fruit May Have Fueled Human Evolution
summary:
Your craving for something sweet might be a very old family tradition — one that helped build the human brain.

A new analysis suggests that simple sugars, like those in fruit and honey, played an overlooked but crucial role in human evolution. The researchers even nicknamed the finding SWEET: sugars were essential in evolution too.

Here's the scale of the change. The brains of our upright-walking ancestors around 4 million years ago weighed only about 300 grams — roughly a medium apple. Today the human brain averages 1,500 grams, about 1.5 liters of water. Much of that expansion happened before early humans mastered fire and cooking.

Until now, much of the story focused on meat. Around 2.5 million years ago, our ancestors began eating more meat — raw at first, then cooked — and that protein and fat seemed to fuel bigger brains. But Jennie Brand-Miller, a nutrition scientist at the University of Sydney, wondered about sugars. A 2017 study had shown fruit-eating primates had bigger brains than leaf-eating ones. Why? Finding ripe fruit is mentally demanding. "You need to remember when various species of ripe fruit begin to ripen, then you need to remember where it is in the forest," Brand-Miller explains. "Your memory is associated with a bigger brain."

Her team calculated the dietary needs of chimps, humans, and three early ancestor species, combining data from fossils, teeth, metabolism, and biology. Our earliest chimp-like ancestors, around 4 million years ago, were largely vegetarians — and fruit likely provided more than two-thirds of their food energy.

Not everyone agrees on the framing. Archaeologist Julie Lee-Thorp says a focus on meat may reflect a modern bias: "Meat is a high-status food today, and that has perhaps been carried over into the way we think about the past." Biological anthropologist Brian Wood argues the field hasn't been meat-obsessed, and that many foods — fruit, honey, nuts, underground plant parts — mattered.

Either way, sugars and meat look like parallel stories, not rivals. "Animal foods were clearly important," Brand-Miller says. So was fruit.
why_it_matters: How we tell the story of our own origins shapes what we call a 'natural' diet today, so a debate about fruit versus meat is also a debate about how scientific assumptions get carried into public health advice and popular ideas about what humans are 'meant' to eat.

background_read: Humans and chimpanzees share an ancestor that lived several million years ago, and the fossil record shows that our ancestors' brains expanded dramatically afterwards — an unusual change among mammals. The scientists who study this are palaeoanthropologists, who work from fossils (preserved bones and teeth) and from comparisons with living primates such as chimpanzees (our closest living relatives).

Jennie Brand-Miller works at the University of Sydney in Australia and is best known for research on how quickly different foods raise blood sugar. Julie Lee-Thorp is an archaeologist who reads chemical traces preserved in ancient teeth and bones to work out what early humans ate, while Brian Wood is a biological anthropologist who studies living hunting-and-gathering communities.

The argument the article describes is an old one in the field: did meat or plant foods fuel the growth of the human brain? Much of that brain growth happened before our ancestors mastered fire and cooking, which makes the question of what they could digest raw even more important.

Two warnings about the sweet-tooth angle: wild fruit and honey are very different from the sugary snacks people eat today, and diet evidence from millions of years ago is indirect, built from comparisons and models rather than from a menu.

perspectives.description: Adding sugars to the picture explains why humans are so drawn to sweet tastes and gives fruit and honey real weight in the story of our big brains. It also turns a simple craving into a connection with ancestors millions of years old, which is a satisfying and testable idea.

The diet models are built from fossils, teeth and metabolism rather than from watching what ancient humans ate, so the conclusions are probabilistic. Archaeologist Julie Lee-Thorp also warns that the meat story may simply echo today's food values, where meat is treated as high-status — a reminder that scientists are not immune to modern bias.

Biological anthropologist Brian Wood points out that fruit, honey, nuts and underground plant parts all mattered, and Brand-Miller agrees animal foods were important too. The pattern in this kind of debate is that single-cause explanations rarely survive the evidence; mixed diets are usually the safer answer.

The next steps are more fossil data, better physiological models and studies of how living primates forage, which could test how much brain power really goes into finding fruit. Meanwhile, the sweet-tooth framing should not be read as a health message: wild fruit is not the same as modern sugary food.
